theory.title: MITM: When the Server Is Not Who It Claims
theory.recap: TLS authenticates the server via a certificate. But what if someone intercepts the connection before TLS begins and presents a fake certificate? That is a man-in-the-middle attack - and it succeeds only if the client accepts the fake certificate.
theory.plainObjective: Complete the TCP handshake, then choose the correct TLS path. One path leads to a MITM proxy presenting a forged certificate. The HSTS-protected path leads directly to the real server. Read the labels carefully.
theory.summary: HSTS (HTTP Strict Transport Security) defeats MITM by instructing browsers to never connect via HTTP and to reject all certificate errors - no exceptions. A site with HSTS preloaded in browsers cannot be intercepted even on a compromised network.

bodyParagraphs.heading: How MITM attacks work
bodyParagraphs.text: An attacker positions themselves between your device and the server. They intercept your TCP connection and present their own certificate. If you accept it, they see all your traffic as plaintext before forwarding it.

bodyParagraphs.heading: Certificate validation defeats MITM
bodyParagraphs.text:
TLS certificate validation is the defense. The browser checks:
  • Is the certificate signed by a trusted CA?
  • Does the domain name match?
  • Is it within its validity period?
A MITM must forge all three - which requires compromising a CA.

bodyParagraphs.heading: HSTS: preemptive defense
bodyParagraphs.text:
HSTS tells the browser to always use HTTPS and refuse to connect on any certificate error. The response header is:
Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains
HSTS preload goes further: browsers ship with a list of HSTS sites baked in.

bodyParagraphs.heading: Certificate pinning
bodyParagraphs.text: Pinning hardcodes a specific certificate or CA into an application. Even if a fraudulent CA issues a cert for your domain, a pinned app rejects it. Downside: if your real cert changes, you must update the app.

theory.mission:
Your packet connects to secure.example.com (10.70.1.10) on port 443.

Complete the TCP handshake, then face a TLS fork. The left path is a MITM proxy with a forged certificate. The HSTS path (right) connects directly to the legitimate server with a valid certificate. Choose wisely.

termIntroductions.headline: Man-in-the-Middle
termIntroductions.body: A MITM attacker intercepts your connection before TLS begins. They establish one TLS session with you and another with the real server - acting as a transparent proxy. If you accept their certificate, they see all your plaintext. Your defense: verify the certificate.

termIntroductions.headline: Two Paths, One Real Server
termIntroductions.body: Two exits: the MITM proxy (up) presents a self-signed certificate for this domain - technically a valid TLS connection but not to the real server. The HSTS path (right) connects directly to the real server with a CA-signed certificate. HSTS prevents your browser from ever taking the upper path.

termIntroductions.headline: MITM Certificate Detected
termIntroductions.body: This certificate is self-signed - not issued by a trusted Certificate Authority. A real TLS client rejects it immediately. With HSTS, browsers don't even give you the option to click through the warning. The connection is aborted. Go back and take the HSTS-protected path.

termIntroductions.headline: HSTS
termIntroductions.body: HSTS (HTTP Strict Transport Security) tells browsers to always use HTTPS and refuse ALL certificate errors with no override. The browser already knows this server requires HSTS (it is preloaded). It refuses to connect via the intercepted path - taking you directly to the legitimate TLS handshake.
